entry.title: Technical documentation updates — and where that annual requirement actually comes from

link.title: Technical documentation updates — and where that annual requirement actually comes from

entry.content:
Technical file (TF) and technical documentation (TD) updates sit at the centre of every change impact assessment, and they come round again each year regardless of whether anything has changed. How significant a change is determines whether it lands as a substantial or a minor revision to the TD/TF.

What counts as a significant change. Some changes clearly push a TF update into substantial territory:

  • Sterilization method — for example, moving from ethylene oxide to electron beam radiation
  • Device design
  • Intended purpose
  • Patient population
  • Critical materials that come into contact with the device
  • Anything affecting the overall safety of the device

Food for thought: where does the annual update requirement actually come from? No regulation explicitly states that you must update your TF/TD every year. The requirement is cumulative; it emerges from reading several clauses together.

Under MDR:

  • Article 86(1) requires manufacturers of Class IIb and Class III devices to update the PSUR at least annually, and the regulation states that the PSUR forms part of the technical documentation under Annexes II and III.
  • Article 61(11) requires the clinical evaluation and its documentation to be updated throughout the device lifecycle using PMCF and PMS data. For Class III and implantable devices, the PMCF Evaluation Report and the SSCP, where indicated, must be updated at least annually.

Under MDD:

  • MDD 93/42/EEC states that the clinical evaluation and its documentation must be actively updated with data obtained from post-market surveillance.
  • MDD-certified products today are generally legacy devices under MDR Article 120. MDCG 2021-25 Rev.1 confirms that, in accordance with Article 120(3d), the MDR requirements relating to post-market surveillance, market surveillance, vigilance, and registration of economic operators and devices apply to legacy devices — a provision unchanged by Regulation 2023/607.
  • Follow that back to Article 86, and the annual update applies here too.

Taken together, a 12-month update cycle for the TD/TF is the approach that holds up.

Start from what triggered the change. Read the new change being introduced, how it prompted a regulatory action (change notice/technical file update), and note every deliverable that falls out of it. That list becomes the spine of the update.

Update the documents that hang off the change. Validation/aging/quality inspection reports, product specifications, the GSPRC, labeling. Work through each one and either update it or create it new so it reflects the change.

Bring subject matter experts in early. Get the right reviewer onto the right section: a sterilization SME on the sterilization sections; a regulatory compliance review of the standards and GSPRC clauses the device is declared against with its evidence of completion. Early alignment saves rework later.

Redline everything, then get it peer-reviewed. Capture every change in redlines, with background information where it helps. Peer review is the critical step; it’s what confirms the changes were captured accurately and that the change history carries sufficient rationale.

Don’t release until the deliverables are closed. Before releasing the technical documentation into the regulatory repository, confirm that all reports, document and labeling updates are complete and released in the quality system. If something is still pending, either work with the change owner to close it first, or assess the risk and agree the strategy from there.

Expect the Declaration of Conformity to follow. The next deliverable after a TD update is usually the impact to the DoC, and the change type normally answers it for you. Adding a manufacturing site, for example, changes the content of the DoC, which means it has to be re-signed by the authorized signatory to stay compliant with the latest changes.
entry.summary: Technical file (TF) and technical documentation (TD) updates sit at the centre of every change impact assessment, and they come round again each year regardless of whether anything has changed. How significant a change is determines whether it lands as a substantial or a minor revision to the TD/TF.

entry.title: A deeper dive into addendum labeling

link.title: A deeper dive into addendum labeling

entry.content:
In my earlier post on the EU MDD to EU MDR transition, I promised a closer look at addendum labeling. It’s one of the most timeline-sensitive parts of a product launch, and getting ahead of it can save enormous time in making the device reach patients.

What addendum labeling covers. It’s any label (carton, pouch, MRP sticker, importer label, CH-REP/CH-Importer label) or labeling (Instructions for Use, patient guide, implant card) created to meet a country’s regulatory and language requirements. These requirements and the labeling change from country to country.

Identify country-specific requirements early. The biggest lever is pinning down requirements during the registration/submission stage, then confirming with affiliates that they’re still current:

  • Use internal procedures to understand requirements and watch for emerging changes. E.g., CALA markets like Brazil and Mexico have traditionally required paper IFUs, but Mexico now accepts eIFU thanks to a new emerging issue. Closing the gap between RA and affiliates on current requirements early prevents surprises later.

Match the submission type to your labeling plan. Look at how the submission affects labeling — is it a new registration/license, or an amendment to the existing one? For an amendment, the license number often stays the same, so labels like import and product labels can often be created ahead of approval. This matters because some countries take 3–6 months to approve; if labeling takes a similar amount of time, starting only after approval pushes the launch timelines out.

  • Get draft labels released ahead of time so the final version can go out quickly once approval lands, agreeing timelines with the affiliate early on what can start before approval.
  • IFUs or patient guides are trickier, since authority feedback often comes closer to approval, so they can’t always start early.

Get the IFU and labeling content right. For country-specific IFUs:

  • Compare the latest draft against the previous approved version to confirm everything aligns with local requirements and applicable regulations such as MDR.
  • Add country specifics — e.g. adding storage-specific info per ANVISA’s requirements for Brazil labeling.
  • Redline every change with comments and explanations so deviations are visible and aligned with the affiliate and authority.
  • Have check points, such as the applicability of CE/UKCA marking for certain EMEA countries — e.g., Ukraine expects its own conformity assessment mark instead of the above markings; the same care applies to Authorized Rep details.
  • Keep approval letters and the relevant regulations on file as evidence for anything added/deleted. Confirm with the affiliate before proceeding.

Implement across the supply chain. Work with the labeling team, international affiliates, supply chain, and distribution centers in parallel for visibility into completion and realistic launch timelines, and so that, once labeling is implemented, country-specific labeling is applied to, or provided with the product before it ships. Incorrect labeling can mean non-compliance, a hold at customs, and ultimately delayed availability to the patient.

(This approach applies not just to the MDD-MDR transition but also to change impact assessments more broadly.)
entry.summary: In my earlier post on the EU MDD to EU MDR transition, I promised a closer look at addendum labeling. It’s one of the most timeline-sensitive parts of a product launch, and getting ahead of it can save enormous time in making the device reach patients.

entry.title: Learnings from global submissions - EU MDD to EU MDR transition

link.title: Learnings from global submissions - EU MDD to EU MDR transition

entry.content:
Regulatory affairs leans heavily on cross-functional teams, which makes timely communication one of the most critical factors in getting devices to patients on time for their treatment. Here are the lessons that made the biggest difference to me during an EU MDD to EU MDR transition.

Collaborate with affiliates early. The single most important step in a successful EU MDD to EU MDR transition is engaging affiliates early in the process. Early collaboration gives you clarity on:

  • Country-specific submission requirements
  • Emerging issues and evolving regulations
  • Documents likely to be delayed
  • Distributor processes

Whenever I spot a gap in my understanding of what’s needed, I ask affiliates for examples or templates. I also use previous submissions as a baseline — they show what the regulatory authority accepted before and help me anticipate the kinds of queries we’re likely to receive.

Handle regulatory authority responses methodically. When a response comes back from the authority, my go-to approach is to:

  • Schedule a meeting with the affiliate to fully understand what the authority is asking for
  • Ask for examples of similar questions raised previously for other portfolios, and how we addressed them
  • Prioritize these requests as they arrive — authority responses usually carry a fixed 30-day deadline

Addendum labeling. The process starts with understanding the timelines for addendum labeling implementation, then assessing the impact to the license number — whether it stays the same (e.g., an amendment) or changes (e.g., a new registration) — and weighing whether to start addendum labeling creation earlier in the process.

(A deeper dive into addendum labeling is coming in a separate post.)

Communicate delays as soon as you know. Flag delays to affiliates the moment you become aware of them. Early notice lets you build mitigation strategies together — for example, submitting certain documents later in the submission process as agreed upon by the authority. It also helps you understand the full impact of a delay: penalties, timeline slippage, and business impact.

Give teams a heads-up before a big wave of submissions. When a large volume of submissions is coming, notify the teams involved — supply chain, manufacturing, labeling, and others — about the upcoming submissions and LBEs. That way they can prepare well in advance and know what to expect.
entry.summary: Regulatory affairs leans heavily on cross-functional teams, which makes timely communication one of the most critical factors in getting devices to patients on time for their treatment. Here are the lessons that made the biggest difference to me during an EU MDD to EU MDR transition.
